"Al-yusra" (ease) is the good and pleasing condition in this world and the Hereafter, and "al-'usra" (hardship) is the evil condition in this world and the Hereafter, inevitably. Whoever makes "bakhila" (was stingy) specific to wealth also makes "istaghna" (considered himself self-sufficient) specific to wealth, so that the blame may be magnified. Whoever makes "bakhila" general to everything one ought to give of word and deed says: "istaghna" means he considered himself independent of Allah the Exalted and His mercy, by his own assumption. Then the Exalted specified the place where his wealth will not avail him at the time of his fall, and this indicates that the giving and the stinginess mentioned are concerning wealth.

People differed about the meaning of "taraddaa" (falls). Qatada and Abu Salih said: its meaning is that he falls into Hell, that is, he falls from its edges. Mujahid said: "taraddaa" means he perishes, from "al-radaa" (destruction). Some people said: its meaning is that he is wrapped in his shrouds, from "al-ridaa" (cloak). From this is the saying of Malik ibn al-Rayb:

"My resting place was pierced by the points of spears, and the excess of my cloak was returned over my eyes."

From this is the saying of another:

"Your share of what you gather throughout your life are two cloaks in which you are wrapped, and camphor."

Then the Exalted informed that upon Him is the guidance of all people, meaning making them know all the paths and granting them understanding, as the Exalted said: ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾ [al-Nahl: 9]. Then each person after that earns what has been decreed for him. This guidance is not the guidance of direction to faith, for if it were so, no disbeliever would exist. Then He informed that the Hereafter and the first life are both under His dominion, meaning which of the two abodes.

As for His saying, ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾, it is either an address from Him, glory be to Him, or it means: say to them, O Muhammad. The majority of the seven readers recited "tala ẓẓa" (tala-zza) with a light "ta'" (tatalaẓẓa, i.e., tala-zza with a single t). Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, recited it with a doubled "ta'" and assimilation of the "ra'" into it, and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited it the same way. It is also narrated from him "tatalaẓẓa" with two "ta's," and Ibn al-Zubayr and Talha recited likewise.

As for His saying, ﴿none will burn in it except the most wretched﴾, meaning: none will burn in it with the burning of eternal abiding. From here the Murji'a (a sect that deferred judgment of sinners) went astray, because they took the negation of burning absolutely, in its little and much. "Al-ashqa" (the most wretched) here means the disbeliever, as evidenced by His saying: "who denies," and the Arabs make the form "af'al" in the place of "fa'il" for emphasis, as Tarafa said:

"Men wish that I die, and if I die, that is a path in which I am not the only one."

The people of interpretation did not differ that what is meant by "al-atqa" (the most righteous), up to the end of the surah, is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. Then the description includes everyone who enters these attributes. As for His saying, ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾, its meaning is: he purifies himself and grows. The apparent meaning of this wording is that it is about the recommended acts (mandubat, acts whose performance is rewarded but whose omission is not sinful). As for His saying, ﴿and no one has a favour with him﴾ and so on, its meaning is: his giving is not so that he may be repaid for blessings that were bestowed upon him; rather, he initiates it seeking the countenance of Allah the Exalted.

It is related regarding the cause of this that the Quraysh said, when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, freed Bilal: "Bilal had a favour with him." Al-Tabari went to the view that the meaning is: he does not give in order to be rewarded with blessings for which he expects recompense someday and awaits its reward. He wandered around this meaning and circled it with lengthy, unproductive elaboration. The meaning that he intended is more directly suggested by a simpler statement than his, namely that the sense is: no one has with him any giving so that there may fall to him from that person any recompense afterward; rather it is purely for the reward and recompense of Allah the Exalted.

As for His saying, ﴿except seeking﴾, "ibtigha'" is in the accusative by a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not from the same category), and there is some debate about it. "Ibtigha'" means seeking. Then the Exalted promised him His good pleasure in the Hereafter, and this is a promise to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Mas'ud (or some readers) recited "yurda" with a "y" pointed for the passive form. This verse resembles the pleasure in His saying: ﴿O soul at rest, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him]﴾ [al-Fajr: 27–28].

The commentary of Surah [al-Layl] is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
